svg.text: C1-A DOOR HATCH WITH AIRLOCK — vestibule in a replacement door (rejected)
A small chamber with an inner and an outer flap, never open together, lets the box out sideways into a shaft between the shells.
per opening: fridge 0.3 kJ, freezer 0.75 kJ
retrieval ≈ 22 s, outer flap open ≈ 3 s
costs +220 mm of wall, 2 drives per shell
FRONT SECTION OF THE COLD MODULE
ZOOM: the vestibule at the top of the fridge door
WHY THE AIRLOCK: a door opening is vertical
the box leaves sideways, so the doors must face a
shaft: +220 mm of wall (1,420 instead of 1,200)
2 extra drives per shell: flap cam, vestibule belt
humid air frosts the vestibule: daily 10 min warm-up
at 10 W and a drain to the evaporation tray
doors face the shaft: people cannot open them;
service means lifting a door off its hinges
about €655 per shell plus the shaft frame
Verdict: thermally good, but it needs a front or
side transport lane that K9b does not have.

g.text: 1/7 The shells are turned 90°: both doors face a shared shaft. The replacement fridge door carries a vestibule (airlock) at the top level.
2/7 The S4 carriage inside brings the box up to the vestibule level; the cam opens the inner flap.
3/7 The carriage pushes the box into the vestibule; the inner flap closes behind it. Both flaps are never open together.
4/7 Only now the outer flap opens: just the vestibule's 10.6 L of cold air spill into the shaft, not the fridge's air.
5/7 A floor belt pushes the box onto the ledge, the outer flap closes, and the gallery hoist dips into the shaft to pick it.
6/7 Every cycle brings humid room air into the vestibule: in the freezer it frosts up, needs a daily warm-up and a drain.
7/7 The price: the shaft costs 220 mm of wall, two extra drives per shell, and people can no longer open the doors.
